Technical Model

Section 02 — Acceleration

Physics of Speed — Two Lenses

Kinetics
The study of forces acting on or produced by an object — what causes the motion.
Kinematics
The properties of motion in an object, without reference to the forces causing it — what the motion looks like.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Scalar vs. Vector — And Inertia

Scalar
Magnitude only, no direction. Speed and distance are scalars — e.g. "8 m/s" or "40 yards" — useful, but incomplete for coaching technique.
Vector
Magnitude and direction. Acceleration and velocity are vectors — e.g. "8 m/s forward" or "3.5 m/s² horizontal" — direction is half the information.
Newton's 1st Law — Inertia
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at the same speed and in the same direction, unless acted on by an unbalanced force. A sprinter in the blocks is inertia waiting to be overcome — that first force application is the whole game.
Section 02 — Acceleration

The Governing Formulas

Velocity
Distance ÷ Time
Bolt, 2008: 10m in 1.685s (reaction time removed) → 5.93 m/s average horizontal velocity.
Acceleration
ΔVelocity ÷ ΔTime
(5.93 m/s − 0)/1.685s → 3.52 m/s² average horizontal acceleration.
Force
Mass × Acceleration
82kg athlete, 0→6 m/s in 0.65s → ~757N average horizontal force.
Newton's 2nd Law — Force
The acceleration of an object produced by a net force is directly proportional to the force, acts in the same direction as the force, and is inversely proportional to the object's mass. Heavier athletes need proportionally more horizontal force to hit the same acceleration — one reason relative strength, not just absolute strength, predicts start quality.
Section 02 — Acceleration

The Formulas, Applied

The Phases, In Real Data — Bolt, 100m, 2015 Beijing World Championships
Even elite max velocity doesn't last — note the drop after 80m. This is the 3-Second Window in real data, not just theory.
Source: Mackala, K. (2013). A Kinematics Analysis of Three Best 100 m Performances Ever. Journal of Human Kinetics, 36(1), 149–160. [6]

Section 02 — Acceleration

The Start Checkpoint, In Real Data

Horizontal Start Velocity — Block Clearance Through Step 2
Notice the flat spots at each ground contact (0.36–0.42s, 0.60–0.66s, 0.84–0.90s) — velocity briefly plateaus at touchdown before the next push resumes it.
Source: Mann, R. (2011). [4]
Section 02 — Acceleration

Does It Matter How Quickly We Generate Force?

Yes
Ground contact during acceleration lasts roughly 0.1–0.2s. Absolute maximum strength can take 0.6–0.8s to develop — far longer than any contact will last. Rate of force development (RFD), not maximum strength, determines how much force an athlete actually gets to use in that window.
Force Development Over Time — By Training Background
Two athletes can share the same maximum strength and still produce very different amounts of force in a 200ms sprint contact — the explosive-ballistic-trained curve is already near its ceiling by 150–200ms, while the untrained curve is still climbing at 500ms.
Concept adapted from Häkkinen, Alen & Komi (1985), as presented in Joyce & Lewindon, High-Performance Training for Sports, Ch. 20.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Acceleration Collapses Toward Zero

Bolt, 100m, 2015 Beijing World Championships — Acceleration by 10m Segment
Acceleration peaks around 20m, then collapses fast — by 70-90m it's essentially zero (max velocity, no longer speeding up), and the final segment goes negative — actual deceleration, even for the fastest man ever timed.
Source: Mackala, K. (2013). A Kinematics Analysis of Three Best 100 m Performances Ever. Journal of Human Kinetics, 36(1), 149–160. [6]

Section 02

Coaching Model

The Coaching Pyramid — Posture → Leg Action → Arm Action — and the cues that fix each level.

Section 02 — Acceleration

The Coaching Pyramid

Section 02 — Acceleration

Coaching Cues — Posture

  • Cue"Nose to toes, straight as it goes" — whole-body rigidity from the neck through the drive leg.
  • Cue"Lean like you mean it" — reinforces the forward lean without collapsing at the hips.
  • Cue"Long and strong" — prevents premature trunk extension out of the drive phase.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Coaching Cues — Leg Action — Front Side

  • Cue"Quick knee, low ceiling" — a quick, low recovery knee, not a high exaggerated lift.
  • Cue"Break the glass" — an aggressive, fast ground strike rather than a passive placement.
  • Cue"Punch the pad" — drives the front knee toward a target, keeping recovery quick and mechanical.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Coaching Cues — Leg Action — Back Side

  • Cue"Rip it back" — full hip extension rather than a passive toe-off.
  • Cue"Attack the ground" — maximal effort at the moment of ground contact, not just after.
  • Cue"Push back, not down" — reframes the push as horizontal force, not vertical bounding.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Coaching Cues — Arm Action

  • Cue"Whip it back" — aggressive backward arm drive, not a forward reach.
  • Cue"Down, and back" — reinforces the backward-and-down elbow path, not a circular swing.
  • Cue"Split and drive" — cues the arms to work in opposition to the legs, maintaining separation rather than syncing forward together.
Section 02 — Acceleration

Coaching Cues — Integration

  • Cue"Power before speed" — prioritizes force production over turnover rate early in the drive phase.
  • Cue"Move the Piston" — reinforces synchronized, linear arm-leg drive rather than loose, floppy limbs.
  • Cue"Stay tall, stay tight" — whole-body tension and size through the drive, preventing collapse under fatigue.

Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Max Velocity, Defined

Tall Posture
~10° upright, front-side hip flexion, neutral hips.
Minimal Oscillation
Bouncing wastes energy that should go toward horizontal propulsion.

The goal here shifts: not producing more force, but maintaining mechanics as fatigue starts to bite.

Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Technical Goals

Goal 01
Synchronize & Maximize Hip Flexion
Synchronize front and backside leg action with arm action in an effort to maximize the peak hip flexion achieved in the front leg.
Goal 02
Minimize Braking, Maximize Vertical Force
Contact the ground as close to the center of mass as possible, minimizing braking forces and maximizing vertical force.

Section 03

Coaching Model

The Coaching Pyramid — Posture → Leg Action → Arm Action — and the cues that fix each level.

Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

The Coaching Pyramid

The same correction model as Acceleration, applied to max-velocity mechanics: Posture → Leg Action → Arm Action — fix the base first, then work up.

Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Coaching Cues — Posture

  • Cue"Stay tall" — the ~10° upright posture target at max velocity, not the forward lean of acceleration.
  • Cue"Cut the breeze" — a subtle forward shin/ankle lean without collapsing at the hips.
  • Cue"Buckle leads the way" — keeps the hips tall and forward rather than sitting back.
Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Coaching Cues — Leg Action — Front Side

  • Cue"Tuck and clear" — a high heel recovery that steps over the opposite knee, not a low shuffle.
  • Cue"Point laces up" — reinforces an active, fast recovery rather than a passive swing.
  • Cue"Knee to the sky"… "Shatter glass" — cues aggressive front-side knee drive into the next stride.
Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Coaching Cues — Leg Action — Back Side

  • Cue"Punch the ground down" — a stiff, active foot strike under the hips, not a reaching touchdown.
  • Cue"Snatch it back" — reinforces a fast, active ground contact rather than a prolonged push.
  • Cue"Turn the wheel" — cues continuous, cyclical leg turnover rather than a start-stop action.
Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Coaching Cues — Arm Action

  • Cue"Punch back" — aggressive backward arm drive to match leg cadence.
  • Cue"Elbow down and back" — reinforces a compact, fast elbow path rather than a wide swing.
  • Cue"Throw the ball back" — a concrete image cue to reinforce the same backward arm snap.
Section 03 — Maximum Velocity

Coaching Cues — Integration

  • Cue"Hold the line under load" — integration cue reinforcing posture under fatigue.
  • Cue"Cut the scissors" — cues the reciprocal front/back leg cycling motion as one continuous action.
  • Cue"Stay above the wheel" — reinforces staying tall over a fast, continuous leg cycle rather than sitting into it.
